name: Abu Simbel
info: Abu Simbel is a pair of rock-cut temples on the western bank of the Nile in Nubia, carved in the 13th century BCE for Ramesses II and his wife Nefertari and moved in 1968 to higher ground to escape the rising waters of Lake Nasser.

facts.made: Ramesses II of the 19th Dynasty, who built the Great Temple for himself and the gods Amun, Ra-Horakhty and Ptah, and the Small Temple for his chief wife Nefertari and the goddess Hathor
facts.form: Two temples cut into a sandstone mountainside; the Great Temple has a façade 33 metres high and 38 metres wide with four seated colossi of about 20 metres, and the Small Temple a façade with statues of slightly more than 10 metres
facts.where: Abu Simbel, Aswan Governorate, Upper Egypt, on the western bank of Lake Nasser near the border with Sudan, on an artificial hill 65 and 67 metres above and 208 metres inland from their original sites
facts.known: the four colossi of Ramesses II; reliefs of the Battle of Kadesh; the stele of the Hittite marriage; the sun striking the sanctuary on two days a year; the Greek graffito of Psamtik II's soldiers; the relocation of 1964 to 1968

t: Ramesses II had the two temples cut into the mountainside in Nubia, a source of gold and other trade goods, to impress upon the Nubians Egypt's might and to Egyptianise them.

Sand covered the Great Temple until European travellers reached it in the early 19th century; Belzoni's party entered it on 1 August 1817, and Champollion's reading of cartouches from drawings made there came in 1822.
In 1964 to 1968 the temples were cut into 1,036 blocks and rebuilt 65 metres higher and 208 metres inland, an operation that helped lead to the UNESCO World Heritage List.
dyk: To save the Great Temple's colossi from the 30-ton lifting limit, the crowns were cut off, and each face was then cut away behind the ears; the first, a 19-ton face, was lifted by crane.
ev: Construction of the temple complex began and lasted for about 20 years, until 1244 BCE
The Swiss researcher Johann Ludwig Burckhardt found the Small Temple and the top frieze of the Great Temple
Giovanni Belzoni's party entered the Great Temple on 1 August after 22 days of work
Royal Engineers removed about 850 long tons of dangerous rock from above the façade
Alessandro Barsanti's clearing of the sand drift, begun in 1909, was completed, exposing a row of statues and the Chapel of Re-Harakhty
An international campaign began to save the monuments of Nubia from the waters of the Aswan High Dam
The first block was lifted out of the Great Temple on 21 May
The relocated complex was finished and formally inaugurated on 22 September

sections.origins:
During his reign Ramesses II embarked on an extensive building programme throughout Egypt and Nubia, which Egypt controlled. Nubia was a major source of gold and many other precious trade goods and was therefore of great importance to the Egyptians. He built several grand temples there in order to impress upon the Nubians Egypt's might and to Egyptianise the people of Nubia. The most prominent were the rock-cut temples near the modern village of Abu Simbel, at the Second Nile Cataract, the border between Lower Nubia and Upper Nubia.

There are two temples. The Great Temple was dedicated to Ramesses II himself, and the Small Temple to his chief wife, Queen Nefertari. Construction of the complex started in c. 1264 BCE and lasted for about 20 years, until 1244 BCE. It was known as the Temple of Ramesses, Beloved by Amun. The Great Temple was dedicated to the gods Amun, Ra-Horakhty and Ptah, Egypt's three state deities of the time, as well as to the deified Ramesses, and the Small Temple to the goddess Hathor, personified by Nefertari. Ra-Horakhty, Amun Ra and Ptah were the main divinities of that period, and their cult centres were at Heliopolis, Thebes and Memphis respectively.
sections.content:
The Great Temple has a single entrance flanked by four colossal statues of Ramesses II, each about 20 metres high, seated on a throne and wearing the double crown of Upper and Lower Egypt. Beside the king's legs stand smaller statues of Nefertari, his mother Mut-Tuy, his first two sons and his first six daughters. The façade behind them is 33 metres high and 38 metres wide. It carries a frieze of twenty-two baboons worshipping the rising sun and a stele recording the marriage of Ramesses to a daughter of King Hattusili III, which sealed the peace between Egypt and the Hittites.

The hypostyle hall is supported by eight Osirid pillars depicting the deified Ramesses linked to Osiris. Its walls bear battle scenes, much of the sculpture being given to the Battle of Kadesh, in which the king fought the Hittites; the most famous relief shows him on his chariot shooting arrows at fleeing enemies. A second pillared hall and a vestibule lead to the sanctuary, where four seated figures are cut into the rear wall: Ra-Horakhty, the deified king, Amun Ra and Ptah.

The Small Temple stands about 100 metres to the northeast. Its façade has statues of the king and queen of slightly more than 10 metres, and it is one of very few instances in Egyptian art where a king and his consort are shown at equal size.
sections.making:
The temples were cut into the rock over about twenty years, and their alignment is the best-known mark of the builders' planning. It is believed that the temple's axis was positioned by the ancient Egyptian architects so that on 22 October and 22 February the sun's rays would penetrate the sanctuary and illuminate the sculptures on the back wall, except for the statue of Ptah, a god connected with the realm of the dead, who always remained in the dark. The dates are allegedly the king's birthday and coronation day, though there is no direct evidence to support this. One calculation, based on the heliacal rising of the star Sirius and on inscriptions, holds that the date must have been 22 October.

The date of the event would have been different when the temple was built, because of the drift of the Tropic of Cancer over about three millennia, and the temple was later moved, so the present alignment may not be as precise as the original. The phenomenon was first reported by Amelia Edwards in 1874, who judged that the effect was calculated and that the excavation was directed at one angle to produce it.

A Greek graffito on the left leg of the southern colossus records the passage of the soldiers of Psamtik II, led by Potasimto, the Egyptians by Amasis, and names Greek and Carian soldiers who scratched their names on the monument.
sections.reception:
With time the temples fell into disuse, and the Great Temple became mostly covered by a sand dune. The temple remained unknown to Europeans until March 1813, when the Swiss researcher Johann Ludwig Burckhardt found the Small Temple and the top frieze of the Great Temple. In 1816 Giovanni Belzoni agreed a wage of two piastres a day per man with the local sheikh and exposed the head and shoulders of two colossi; he returned in 1817, and his party entered the Great Temple on 1 August after 22 days' work. In 1819 William John Bankes led a party that documented the interior.

Drawings made there reached Jean-François Champollion on 14 September 1822, and the first cartouche he could decipher, connected to Ramesses, led, on his account, to his realisation that hieroglyphs mixed symbolic and phonetic signs. He and Ippolito Rosellini copied all the reliefs in 1828. David Roberts sketched the site in 1838, and Maxime Du Camp took the first photographs in 1850.

Visitors also left marks: Isabella Romer cut her name into the throne of the southern colossus in 1845, and Amelia Edwards's party inscribed theirs in the Chapel of Thoth, which Andrew McCallum found on 16 February 1874. Thomas Cook began a steamer service passing Abu Simbel in 1874.
sections.survival:
In December 1892 the Egyptian Department of Public Works found that overhanging rock threatened the colossi. A detachment of Royal Engineers worked from February to April 1893 and removed nearly 850 long tons of dangerous material, without accidents, at less than half the original estimate of £1,000. Between 1909 and 1910, under Alessandro Barsanti, the sand drift was permanently cleared. A row of statues of the pharaoh and the sacred hawk and the Chapel of Re-Harakhty came to light, and the colossi were stabilised with cement and iron pins.

In 1959 an international campaign began to save the monuments of Nubia from the Aswan High Dam, whose lake would raise the water level at Abu Simbel by up to 60 metres. The sandstone would lose its strength once submerged. Several schemes were proposed, and in 1962 UNESCO preferred an Italian plan to lift the temples whole, but Egypt adopted in 1963 a plan from the Swedish firm VBB to cut them into blocks, estimated at US$36 million, half the cost of the others.

After building a cofferdam, workers removed about 300,000 tons of rock, injected the stone with epoxy resin and cut the temples into 1,036 blocks, the last removed on 16 April 1966. The Great Temple was rebuilt 208 metres further inland and 65 metres higher, the Small Temple 67 metres higher, each under a concrete dome beneath an artificial hill. The project was completed in 1968 at a cost of US$41.7 million, about half borne by Egypt and half by contributions from 48 countries.
sections.legacy:
The relocation was considered at the time one of the greatest challenges of archaeological engineering in history. Its success helped the United Nations introduce a convention establishing the UNESCO World Heritage List, and the relocated complex belongs, with Philae, Amada and Wadi es-Sebua, to the World Heritage Site known as the Nubian Monuments. The team confirmed on 22 February 1966 that the sun's rays reached the statues of Ramesses, Amun and Ra-Horakhty in the sanctuary while that of Ptah stayed in shadow, and the temples were oriented to repeat the two annual occasions, within a permitted deviation of 5 millimetres.

The site also shaped the study of ancient Egypt. The drawings made there in 1819 served Champollion in deciphering hieroglyphs, and the photographs of Du Camp, Teynard and Frith in the 19th century belong to the early photographic record of Nubia. Early descriptions and drawings are found in Edward William Lane's Description of Egypt.

The temples remain a place where people gather on 22 October and 22 February to see the sun reach the sanctuary. They stand in the village of Abu Simbel on the western bank of Lake Nasser, about 230 km southwest of Aswan, in a hot desert climate.

summary: Abu Simbel is a pair of rock-cut temples built for Ramesses II and Nefertari from about 1264 BCE in Nubia. Sand buried the Great Temple until European travellers reached it in the 19th century, and in 1964 to 1968 the temples were cut into blocks and rebuilt on higher ground above Lake Nasser.

Lynne Olson, Empress of the Nile: The Daredevil Archaeologist Who Saved Egypt's Ancient Temples from Destruction (Random House, 2023)

notes: The article gives construction as c. 1264 BC to 1244 BC (about 20 years) but also says the Great Temple was completed around year 24 of Ramesses II (1265 BC). The second date was left out; start -1264 with circa true.
The article says the sand 'already covered the statues up to their knees' by the 6th century BC; left out as a date of uncertain meaning.
Nobody 'discovered' the site: the article says it remained unknown to Europeans until 1813 and that Nubian locals were hired for the digging; wording kept to Europeans.
Not used: tourism, visitor numbers, airport, popular culture, the proposals' details beyond the adopted one.
The making section holds little on carving technique because the article has none; it uses the alignment and graffito material.
The article's claim about Edwards: she wrote the effect was calculated; the article also says the dates' birthday/coronation link has no direct evidence; both given.
Isabella Romer is called the first European woman to visit in the article; not used.
